title: Prabhakar Raghavan - Can AI assist in Mathematics and Computer Science research?
transcriptText:

Prabhakar Raghavan.

students know him
originally from his book
on Randomized Algorithms.

to IBM Research.

The next point I want to make

in all these cases is hard.
But the use of fast and sloppy
verifiers within the evolution
loop is a very
powerful technique
provided, at the
end of the day, you
have the means and
the wherewithal
to do an exact
verification, whether it's
through trying all combinations
of Boolean variables,
which we did.
Or you can write a Lean prover
or whatever it is that you want.
So in that sense, one of
our insights here, I think,
is as you're
building up a proof,
you don't have to
be super exact.
You can actually make
progress without it.
Could a talented human have
produced these results?
And we spent a lot of
time debating this.
And when you look at a gadget
on 19 nodes with edge weights
from 1 to 1429, I
would submit that it's
difficult for a human
with a paper and pencil
to come up with that.
This is not a
definitive argument.
I'll also add that when humans
try to handle large objects
and of the sort, they look
for symmetries to speed up
how they think about it.
And the TSP proof, the gadget we
found, was actually asymmetric.
I should have pointed
this out, but the gadget
is somewhat asymmetric
and not the first thing
that you as a human
might think of.
Obviously, it's
difficult for me to argue
that no human could have
matched our AI-assisted proofs.
And in fact, it's entirely
possible some of these results
will be improved by human
giving a much simpler proof
than we have.
Just the fact that we found
a large gadget doesn't
mean that everybody has
to find a larger gadget.
On the one result, I
showed in the average case,
hardness of Max-Cut.
It did need a larger graph,
and we've hit the limit,
so I don't expect
humans to improve that.
So ultimately, I think what will
judge us is the test of time.
Because you do see a lot of
reports of AI-assisted proofs
quickly get superseded by
humans saying, yeah, I did that.
I went off to think
about it for a day
and I found the same thing.
And conversely,
people do say, well, I
could have done this in a day.
I think Timothy Gowers
had a tweet that said,
something that would
have taken me a week,
the LLM helped me do
in a couple of days.
But that to me is not, in some
sense, a superhuman capability.
So I want to submit
that AlphaEvolve,
in the incarnation of generating
programs that generated
pieces of proofs,
has in these cases
done something interesting.
It's broken the state of the
art, and the test of time
will decide if that
remains the best possible.
Now, could comparable computing
have succeeded without AI?
And again, it's difficult to
give you a definitive answer.
What I can tell you is that
for the kinds of proofs
we were looking at,
we tried a bunch
of alternative formulations
through SAT solvers
and through math
programming methods.
And we couldn't
come close to these
because the scales
just exploded on us.
Now, you could
counter that by saying
that's because you're
not very smart the way
you do math programming
or whatever.
And in fact, the earliest
advance of this type
were due to a piece of work
that used linear programming.
And I'll come to
that in a second.
There's this interesting
note recently put out
by Elchanan Mossel,
who says, look,
if you're going to claim that
something was done with AI,
you should have a criterion for
being able to refute that claim.
Otherwise, it's not fair.
And moreover, if
you're going to claim
something was done with AI, it
should be a fully replicable
experiment.
And in that sense, we're
still a work in progress.
There's a lot of work out there
saying I prompted interactively
for a week and got somewhere.
And Mossel makes this
point that unless you're
replicating every prompt and
showing people what you've done,
it's a little difficult
to describe that
as a scientific experiment.
And I think that's
a good argument.
I did mention that some of
the early work of this style,
on proving hardness of
approximation results,
use linear programming.
And this is almost 30 years
old now by Trevisan et al.
So we were inspired by them.
It's just that we thought
that math programming had
hit its limits, which is why
we reached out to AlphaEvolve.
So we've struggled to
understand what AlphaEvolve
is doing in the innards.
The one thing it does seem like
using the model to evolve code
to print out proof
fragments seems
more powerful than
asking the model
to print out proof fragments.
We did actually-- and
I'll say a little bit more
on this in a second.
But the feeling
we had repeatedly
is you have a fleet of research
assistants, maybe thousands,
to try various approach.
And especially, this was
evident in the Ramsey search
that we had.
But we don't yet have an
understanding of why it wins
or even whether this
interaction, where an LLM prints
out programs that print out
gadgets or Ramsey graphs,
is really the most
optimized one.
In fact, we're trying to build
a system that does better.
And I know that Berkeley
is one of the places that
was participant in this
program called EvoX that
is an improvement, I
believe, on AlphaEvolve,
that has some nice new
ideas and, I think,
that has some legs ahead.
So people often
ask, why don't you
just prompt the LLM to find the
gadgets or the Ramsey graphs?
And this was a dismal
failure, I'll say.
We couldn't come close.
On the first
anecdote I gave you,
even with straightforward
stochastic differential
equations, the state of
the art models struggled.
And unless you do the
hard math yourself,
it's hard to claim a theorem.
For the latter two pieces
of work I talked about,
hardness of
approximation and Ramsey,
we tried hard and got nowhere.
We made no progress at all.
And in fact, in some cases, we
couldn't reconstruct the state
of the art, even
though that should have
been in the model training.
I'm often asked, how much
computing did you use?
And surely, you guys
are experts and that's
why you were able to do this.
And these are valid questions.
I think we're early
enough in the journey
that I'm not sure there's
the right question.
You're asking whether
it's barely feasible.
The answer to the question, how
much computing, we used lots.
[LAUGHTER]
And it came to the point where
I've said to the team, look,
we should stop burning
cycles because we're burning
cycles out of ignorance.
And we learned a lot.
And so we're getting a
little more sophisticated.
[CLEARS THROAT]
I dare say some of the
earliest results we got,
we could probably speed up
by a factor of 100 soon.
That's because we
made so many mistakes.
So there will come a time to
calibrate, OK, how much compute
did you burn to get a theorem?
I don't think we're there yet.
In terms of how
much expertise, I
hadn't thought
about Ramsey numbers
very much until
a few months ago.
And I'm not an expert in
hardness of approximation,
one of my co-authors maybe.
But I don't think it
was just our expertise
powering these results,
that we're actually
getting some mileage from this.
So it remains to be seen over
time exactly what we're getting.
Now there's other ways,
stepping back a bit.
Many of you have seen AI
help math/CS research.
So you can say, hey,
I'm an expert in algebra
and I want to get familiar
with Ramsey theory.
And the LLM will write a
beautiful 60-page summary
of the state of the art--
10-page if you want, whatever,
and give you a pretty good idea
of the state of the
art in this field.
When we tried, we often got
useful summaries but also
a lot of nonsense.
And we were constantly
lectured about--
models would tell us to
use quantum entanglement
to do something or the other.
And I'm like, I don't know how
to use quantum entanglement.
But I do think this is avenue
is going to be useful over time
because a non-expert can
quickly approach a field,
and this will lead to
more cross-fertilization
across disciplines.
And I think this is a
very powerful thing.
You can get suggestions
on attacking a problem.
Why didn't you try this?
We did not get useful cues.
And I would venture
that the results we have
are beyond such direct LLM use.
Well, you suggest an approach,
and let's go back and forth
a bit.
Obviously, I'm not able to
give you a proof of that.
Now out there in the social
media and the popular media,
you see lots of
claims of, well, I've
solved this problem using AI.
And one of the
things I've noticed
is that you see this
less with problems
that have been around and
studied heavily to attack
using direct LLM prompting.
And even within our
use of AlphaEvolve,
some cells fell
faster than others,
including things where you might
say that's a more obscure cell,
so maybe people didn't
pay much attention to it.
So it doesn't seem
to have strictly
to do with some notion of
how much attention it got.
There's something else.
And especially with the
small Ramsey numbers,
I actually think it has to do
with the modular characteristics
of the two integers
being studied.
So I began with the
quote from du Sautoy.
And one of the things he said--
this was almost 25 years ago--
is computers are going
to be a powerful ally,
but they're never going to
replace human mathematicians.
And that led me to
wonder, what is it
that we think of as human
mathematician's doing?
And this is a very nice
essay by Bill Thurston
from about 30 years ago that
some of you may have seen.
And in this essay, he says,
"The question is not even
how do mathematicians make
progress in mathematics?
Rather," he says, "I prefer, how
do mathematicians advance human
understanding of mathematics?"
And I began thinking about this.
And if someone comes
to you and says,
I have a billion-line Lean code
proof of Fermat's Last theorem.
Have they advanced
mathematics in any way?
And I went to Gemini,
of course, and said,
what's a good way to think
about conceptually, Wiles's
proof of Fermat's Last Theorem?
Then it came back with this.
Personally, I found
this much more
useful than a billion-line
proof because it
does make the connection
between algebraic geometry,
starting with
Weil-Taniyama-Shimura
all the way to Frey curve.
And so to me, it seems
like merely having a proof,
including that 19-node graph,
doesn't necessarily improve
your understanding.
It's somehow a record
that has been held.
One of the things that become
very conscious of in this
is AI models get trained
on success stories,
including proofs that
people published.
The failures don't go into--
they remain in our heads.
And in this sense,
human mathematicians
encapsulate a form of knowledge
that doesn't get into models.
And when we do,
as professionals,
try to prove theorems,
our past failures
actually influence where we go.
And that doesn't get reflected
anywhere in these user models.
So let me go back to a
question that I asked early on.
So should LLMs be
banned from science?
So I would claim that we have
at least one Nobel Prize that
wouldn't have happened without
the use of RL actually,
not LLMs.
And so the genie is out of
the bottle ban, whatever.
And banning models
from science is
a bit like banning microscopes
from biology or telescopes
from astronomy or whatever.
And I was discussing this with a
very senior computer scientist.
And he said, well,
but how do you know
that the results are right?
And if you put your
name on the author list,
you're taking
responsibility for it.
But I think he had
a good point, which
was, we will get besieged by
a flood of false bad results.
And who's to mind the ship?
And in fact, there's a sample
from a couple of months ago
that shows that about
20% of new CS papers
show some marker of
LLM-assisted writing.
That's assisted writing that
may be fixing your grammar
or whatever.
But nevertheless, the language
that recurs in those papers
has a repetitive flavor rather
than trying to explain concepts.
Going back to the point
of the mathematician's job
is to make mathematics
more understood.
So some of you may be aware that
arXiv online has implemented
a new policy because there was
a flood of people writing review
papers with LLMs, which served
as a cheap way of boosting
h-indexes for people.
So in computer science,
this is the new policy
because you had these
AI-generated surveys.
Good.
So just to sum up,
LLMs are becoming
complex for vibe research,
lots of potential
for low-quality service.
We are not at a
point, I believe,
where there's some
definitive capability
that AI has provided--
when Move 37 happened
in the second game between
AlphaGo and Lee Sedol,
there was this notion that
experts came together and said,
well, we really think
that's not something
humans should have done.
So I mentioned
sloppy verification.
My best model is
right now, AlphaEvolve
is akin to having a large
number of pretty smart research
assistants and surely seems more
powerful than direct prompting.
I don't think I can
claim to have deepened
human understanding,
even though you
can use models to provide
literature surveys
and so on, and
start the process,
but not actually
arrive at theorems.
And so I feel like this is
a landscape that's changing
so fast with so much to do.
I found this beautiful line
in Alan Turing's paper,
where he talks about
the imitation game.
And he talks about all
the forms of learning,
supervised learning, et
cetera, that are ahead.
But then he concludes with
this wonderful line that says,
"We can only see a
short distance ahead,
but we can see plenty
that needs to be done."
And that's where I feel we are.
Thank you.

segments.text: HOST: Welcome, everybody. I'm very happy to introduce Prabhakar Raghavan. He's one of us. He has a Berkeley PhD. And those of us who students know him originally from his book on Randomized Algorithms. From there, he went to IBM Research.

And then he led Yahoo Research for many years during the time. I know him quite well. And then he went to Google, where he essentially ran all of Google. I think officially, it was the other parts which were not under Google, but I don't know.

Any part of Google you know was under him, and which meant in particular, as he told me this afternoon, that he had no control over his calendar and eventually went to people and said, look, guys, we have to change. They said, OK, what about if you're a CTO?

He said, OK, I'll do that. So he's now CTO at Google. He is in many societies and academies. I don't want to spend more time. I'll let him give his talk. [APPLAUSE] PRABHAKAR RAGHAVAN: Can you hear me at the back? AUDIENCE: Yes, we can hear you.

PRABHAKAR RAGHAVAN: Great. Thanks. So I want to share some experiences we have, trying to do research using language models. And I'm going to begin with a simple warm-up story of some research we started doing, leave you with a question, then get

to the central technical portion, and then spend a fair bit of time reflecting on where we are on this journey. So that's the program for today. So the first little anecdote that I want to share with you has to do with load balancing

in our large-scale systems. You'll see the setting in just a second. This is joint work with Amer Diwan, who's in Google Search, and Eli Upfal, who works at Brown University. So begin with a quick primer on probability and then tell you what it has

to do with load balancing. So if you throw N balls into N bins, then some bin is going to get a massive load but to first order about log and load. But if instead you did the following, when it's time to throw a ball, you pick two bins at random

and always throw in the lighter loaded one. Then the maximum load drops dramatically. And it gets even better if you pick three, four, et cetera, instead of two. So that's the background probability. What does this have to do with serving search queries,

for instance? So you have a stream of requests and you have N serving clusters, as we call them. You don't want any request to wait too long. And so the question you have to decide as queries come in is, to which serving cluster do you assign a query?

That seems like a clean implementation of these balls and bins paradigm, but real life turns out to be a little more complicated. So let me tell you about some of the complications we had to study. So the first complication if you're doing Google search

is you have temporal bursts. And some of the biggest bursts happen during cricket games, as it turns out. Essentially, 2 billion people in Pakistan, India, and Bangladesh are flooding us with queries all of a sudden, especially towards the end of each game.

And long ago, we used to send every query to the nearest data center. And you can see why that's a bad idea. So that's one complication we wanted to study. The second one we wanted to study was actually, queries come in multiple priorities.

There's user queries, which must take the highest priority. There's no way you should delay them. But there's a lot of system queries, like for evaluation of search algorithms, ranking algorithms, and so on. And those take lower priority. So how do you decide

the assignment in the staging of these? And finally, if you're doing this thing about picking the lightest load of multiple randomly chosen servers, you should know their current load. Except you don't. So in fact, you have slightly stale information.

And that leads to very interesting complications. So you want to study this problem through both simulations and theory. And as a modern computer scientist, what do you do? You do what I call vibe research. And my co-author Amer wrote this

long and very polite prompt. This is for the most basic case. But the thing I want you to note is when he gave this to the model, he was actually pretty sloppy. And I hate to say this of my co-author, but at the top, he says power-of-n scheduling.

But by the time he gets to the last paragraph, n turned into d. And then he talks about a different n, which is further down. And this is not that different from the way a professor might talk to their grad student. They're all over the map and yet the student

gets it, being smart. And so we fed this into the model and said, show us what happens. And what comes back is something like this on the right, which says, here's how the load behaves over time. Then we could add in all these other complicating factors.

N goes all of that. You get as many plots as you want. And I think of this as vibe research. I think an increasing amount of systems research is being done in this way. We also wanted to prove theorems here. The models are not that useful. Here's a theorem we

proved about what happens with multiple priorities. The models, I would say, were pretty good at setting up stochastic differential equations. They would guess solutions, but they couldn't actually give you proofs. And so we said, OK, so

we have some simulations. We have some theorems. What do you do then? You submit it to a conference. So we said to the model, take all of this, write a paper. And so it did. And we were ready to submit it to a conference. And then what happened?

We ran into this language at the conference. It said you shall not use language models for your research. And this is not commonplace, but there are conferences that are now-- so we were scratching our heads. Was our use of Gemini part of the methodology

as deemed by the conference organization? And so in the end, what we decided was to redo everything by hand. So we recorded all the simulations by hand, ran them, got exactly the same results. So in this case, the model didn't lie to us.

But it does beg the question, should archival forums restrict AI tools in science? And I have a perspective, which you can probably figure out, but I will share it when I get back to reflecting later in the talk. I will talk about this some more.

So that was the warm-up part. But really, the central focus that I want to have on this is the following. And as soon as I put up this slide, you'll recognize that the question I'm asking is ill-posed. So I'm not asking was AI used to solve the math problem,

because you have plenty of reports in the news media and not so news media, even in published papers that, yes, I used an LLM and it helped me accelerate my thinking and it gave me the suggestion. What I'm really interested in is the question,

do these LLMs endow us with some capability that I couldn't have gotten to as a smart human with plenty of compute? And I realize, this is very hard to settle beyond doubt, but I'm going to take a crack at some of our experience to show you some of

the results we have, and try and argue to you that a smart human with plenty of compute couldn't have gotten them. So there is something going on. That's not a theorem I'm going to claim. There will be theorems you'll see in a second, but that's the

direction of travel. And we're going to do this in two settings, first, the hardness of discrete optimization, which is a well-studied area for, I guess, 30-plus years. And the second is in Ramsey numbers, which is a well-studied area for 100 years now.

And this is joint work with Ansh Nagda, who's a student here at Berkeley, and my colleague at DeepMind, Abhradeep Thakurta. So first, let's start with discrete optimization. And we're going to look at two problem settings. We're going to look at

a problem called Max-Cut and then we're going to look at the Traveling Salesman Problem. I'll dwell on the former because it's easier to explain what's going on. The Traveling Salesman Problem is gradually technical in the result we prove,

so I'll just touch on it lightly and tell you what we managed to do. Now in all of this, we'll use a tool from Google DeepMind that's called AlphaEvolve. After I get you halfway through the first result, I'll explain what AlphaEvolve did.

So bear with me until then, so I tell you what AlphaEvolve is. So let's begin with Max-Cut. So what is the Max-Cut problem? You're given a graph on N nodes in an undirected graph, and I ask you to cut it in two pieces so that you cut as many edges as possible.

It's hard to do. It's hard to even find an approximately nearly exact optimal cut. And you can consider generalizations of this problem where you want to break it into not 2, but 3, 4, 5 pieces, et cetera. And the first result I'm going to show you

talks about breaking a graph into four pieces to maximize the number of edges cut. So what do we actually show? So we show that it is hard to approximate better than 98.7%, approximate the size of the cut. So not only is it-- if the

graph's biggest way of cutting into four pieces has 1,000 edges, even finding a cut of size 987 is going to be hard. That's what this theorem shows. And we do this using what I call a novel gadget reduction. For those of you who are not

familiar with gadget reductions, I'll give you a quick intro in a second. This beats the previous best result of 98.8%. And you're looking at that and saying, oh my God, you used all this compute at Google to beat something by 0.1%. And the answer is yes.

That's what we did. This was more like we're proving something is doable. It's a 10-year-old result. So it did stand some test of time. But yes, indeed, we have small improvement. And this is the first problem we had where we could actually

beat an existing result. So to tell you how we did this, I'm going to take two slides to tell you what a gadget reduction is and then tell you what we did to improve it. So here's how this works. I want to show you that it's hard to cut a graph into four

pieces. I'm going to start with the problem that's known to be hard and create from it an instance of Max-4Cut, with the argument that if you could cut the graph well, then you could solve the original problem, which is unlikely because it's hard.

So what is the original problem we start with? It's called 3LIN4. It's a family of equations in n variables, but every equation has exactly three variables, and all the equations are mod 4. So everything here is 0, 1, 2, or 3. And this is known to be hard.

And the claim we're going to make is from this, we're going to construct an instance of Max-4Cut, namely a graph. And if you could cut that well, you could solve this, which is unlikely. Therefore, you couldn't have done that. So that's the argument.

So how does this actually work? So gadget is a recipe for taking a piece of the source problem, in this case, the family of equations, and constructing a piece of the target problem. So you pick an equation, and a gadget is a recipe that builds

a piece of a graph. And then by gluing together all of these pieces, you build a graph. And the argument will be that if you could break that graph, then you could solve these equations. I'm not going to take you through all the details,

but what I want to focus on is actually, what is this gadget? So AlphaEvolve, this tool that I haven't defined yet, but I will in a second, found a gadget that yielded the result. And here's what the gadget actually looks like. It takes an equation,

x1 plus x2 plus x3, and builds this 19-node graph. That's a pretty big graph. And you do this for every equation. You glue together all the 19-node graphs and you get this massive graph. And the claim is if you could have broken that, then you could have

solved the original instance. So where did this come from? And in fact, these edges have weights from 1 to 1429. 1 to 1429 is what the tool spat out. There's nothing I know that's interesting about 1429. It's a prime number. Other than that, I don't know.

But you should immediately be suspicious. Why do we know this thing works? How do we know it's correct? So verification is a standard hard problem in computer science, and we'll come to that in a couple of slides. So that's the program.

So now I'm going to tell you what actually found this. AlphaEvolve is this tool. And here's what it does. It is maintaining a fleet of programs, in our case Python programs. And these programs are told to go find good gadgets for this problem.

And they crank away. They spit out gadgets. And you use a synthetic scoring function to tell which programs are doing well and which ones are not. You discard the ones that aren't doing well, take the ones that are proceeding well, feed them back to

the language model, and out come a new family of programs. So that is the fundamental loop. So this is essentially an evolutionary process where the fittest programs go back and create fitter programs, and yet all the time studying the gadgets

to see if they-- right? And this ran for, in our first run, a week. Since then, we've gotten better at this, to spit out that gadget that I just showed you. And then we could take that gadget, verify it in a way I'm about to show you. And there's

something interesting going on in the verification, and say we therefore conclude that it is NP-hard to solve Max-4Cut better than 98.7%. So one way to think about it is somebody, way back, wrote a proof that Max-4Cut-- you could take the 10-year-old

result that I talked about-- has a gadget reduction that shows the 98.8%. And what we did was to essentially snip out that gadget that they had and plug in the new gadget. Those of you who like to think about gene editing can think of this as a form

of that, where you snipped out that little piece, plug this in, and then you make the claim. In general, the way you'd verify that a gadget is working is to try every possible way of breaking this graph into four pieces, which is a humongous

number of things to try, and even just at the scale of 19 nodes in the gadget. This is a very slow process. So what we resorted to was we went back to AlphaEvolve and said, can you speed up the verification? And what follows is interesting. So I'm going to

tell you about that. Now before I do that, I just want to reiterate two things. Number 1, the hardness is not for 19 nodes. It's for all N. But also, AlphaEvolve, remember, has some synthetic objective function. It doesn't know it's actually trying

to prove a theorem about cutting graphs into four pieces. And so it is acting completely, in some sense, syntactically and still generating these graphs. So now let's get to the verification, which I think is one of the things that we did that was instructive.

So we're trying to find a verifier for breaking graphs into four pieces. So we made it generate a lot of Max-4Cut instances with varying amounts of edge density and so on. And we said, what's the biggest gadget you can verify within one second?

And why one second? It's a system constant we just chose because exhaustive verification would take a long time. And we did that. And AlphaEvolve comes back and says, here's a verifier. Now, how do you know that verifier is correct? Well, we don't actually.

But what we did was we took the synthetic verifier that AlphaEvolve spits out, checked it on this data set, passed checks. We used a language model to critique the verifier and finally ended up with the verifier that satisfied this property that in one second,

it could say, yep, this is a good gadget or not. Now if you ask me, do you know for sure that this synthetic verifier was good? The answer is no, but it's fast. So it's fast and sloppy. And when you're putting this in the inner loop of AlphaEvolve,

which is going thousands and thousands of times around, it works. However, before we asserted the theorem, we actually did a brute-force verification. So you spend a lot of time at the very end before you write a paper saying this verifier actually is sound.

Well, the verifier isn't sound. The gadget is sound. I still don't know if the verifier is sound. And this was one of our takeaways, which we use consistently in all the results I'm going to show you. Fast and sloppy verification can
